## 2 The scheme and the main result

Use normalized measure \(dx/(2\pi)\) on \(\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\); changing to unnormalized \(L^2\) only changes constants. Write \(S_t=e^{-t\partial_x^3}\), so that \(\widehat{S_tf}(k)=e^{itk^3}\widehat f(k)\). Let \(P_0\) be the mean, \(P=I-P_0\), and define \(D^{-1}=\partial_x^{-1}\) with multiplier \((ik)^{-1}\) for \(k\ne0\) and zero at zero. Set \(D^{-2}=(D^{-1})^2\). Write
\[
\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
\|f\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\langle k\rangle^{2s}|\widehat f(k)|^2,
\qquad \langle k\rangle=(1+k^2)^{1/2}.
\]
Spaces are the completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms, with negative spaces interpreted as distributions. Orthogonality gives the normalized \(L^2\) identity for polynomials and hence for their completions. For mean-zero functions and \(s\ge0\), \(\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\le\|f\|_{H^s}\le2^{s/2}\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\); for \(s<0\), \(2^{s/2}\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\le\|f\|_{H^s}\le\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\). Real-valued means \(\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}\). All time suprema concern continuous representatives; derivative norms are essential suprema. The exact solution is the unique real mean-zero \(C([0,T];H^\gamma)\) solution obtained by smooth approximation, and satisfies the equation distributionally. The constants \(C_M\) may change from line to line and depend on \(\gamma,T,M\), but are uniform in \(n,\tau\) and spectral support.

The equation is
\[
u_t+u_{xxx}=\tfrac12\partial_x(u^2),\qquad u(0)=u_0. \tag{1}
\]
The fixed scheme is \(u^0=u_0\) and
\[
u^{n+1}=S_\tau u^n+F_\tau(u^n)+H_\tau(u^n),\qquad \tau=T/L, \tag{2}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_\tau(f)&=\tfrac16 P[(S_\tau D^{-1}f)^2]-\tfrac16 S_\tau P[(D^{-1}f)^2],\\
H_\tau(f)&=\tfrac13 P[(S_\tau D^{-1}f)D^{-1}F_\tau(f)]
+\tfrac{\tau}{9}(S_\tau D^{-1}f)P_0(f^2)\\
&\quad-\tfrac1{54}\left[S_{\tau-s}D^{-1}[(S_sD^{-1}f)^3]\right]_{s=0}^{s=\tau}\\
&\quad-\tfrac1{27\tau}\left[S_{\tau-s}D^{-2}[(S_{s-\tau}D^{-2}F_\tau(f))(S_sD^{-1}f)]\right]_{s=0}^{s=\tau}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the scheme of [1, Eq. (1.4)], without a spatial frequency cutoff.

**Theorem 1 (Logarithm-free convergence).** Let \(T>0\), \(0<\gamma\le1\), and \(R>0\). For real, mean-zero \(u_0\in H^\gamma(\mathbb T)\) with \(\|u_0\|_{H^\gamma}\le R\), there are \(C,\tau_0>0\), depending only on \(T,\gamma,R\), such that the scheme (2) satisfies
\[
\max_{0\le n\le L}\|u(n\tau)-u^n\|_{L^2}\le C\tau^\gamma
\qquad\text{whenever }\tau=T/L\le\tau_0.
\]

The periodic KdV bounds of Babin–Ilyin–Titi control the exact flow on the initial-data ball. The continuous estimates of [1, Proposition 3.4 and Lemma 7.2] will be used in the stability proof. The logarithmic convergence theorem itself is not used. For the exact twisted solution \(v(t)=S_{-t}u(t)\), set
\[
M=1+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|v(t)\|_{H^\gamma}.
\]
The source statements and the sign transformation giving a bound for \(M\) are recorded below in Section 2.1. No convergence theorem for the numerical scheme is used as an input. Intermediate constants may depend on \(M,\gamma,T\), but never on the timestep or a Fourier support bound.

<!-- PDF page 3 -->

### 2.1 The exact KdV flow

The source [2, Theorems 4.2–4.3, 5.1, 6.3–6.5] treats \(U_t=UU_x+U_{xxx}\) on the same torus, with normalized measure and mean-zero homogeneous Sobolev norms. Theorem 4.2 bounds its Galerkin flows on \([0,T]\) in \(\dot H^s\) by a constant depending only on \(s,T,\|U_0\|_{\dot H^s}\) and an upper bound for \(\|U_0\|_2\). Theorem 4.3 gives a distributional limiting solution with the same bound. Theorems 5.1 (\(s>1/2\)) and 6.3 (\(0<s\le1/2\)) give its uniqueness, \(C([0,T];\dot H^s)\) regularity and continuous dependence. Theorem 6.4 covers \(s=0\), and Theorem 6.5 with \(\theta=0\) states that, for two flows whose initial \(L^2\) norms sum to at most \(B\),
\(\sup_{[0,T]}\|U-\widetilde U\|_2\le C(T,B)\|U_0-\widetilde U_0\|_2\).
Together these results specify the continuous flow and the uniform bounds needed here.

Define \(u(t,x)=-U(t,-x)\). Then \(u_t=-U_t\), \(u_x=U_x\), \(u_{xxx}=U_{xxx}\) at \((t,-x)\), and consequently \(u_t+u_{xxx}=uu_x\). Fourier coefficients become \(\widehat u(k)=-\widehat U(-k)\), preserving every Sobolev norm, reality and zero mean. This transforms the source equation to (1). The norm comparison above transfers all bounds to our \(H^\gamma\) norm. Hence there is \(A(T,\gamma,R)<\infty\) such that every smooth initial datum in the stated ball satisfies \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u(t)\|_{H^\gamma}\le A\). The same bound holds for the limiting solution: for each finite set of frequencies pass to the limit in its finite norm sum, then take the supremum over finite sets. Thus \(M\le1+A(T,\gamma,R)\) uniformly. Continuous dependence in \(L^2\) is precisely the input used in the final density passage. No change of torus length or amplitude scaling is needed.


## Supplied proof route

The following sentences are transcribed from the supplied paper's abstract/introduction:

"The main estimate concerns the exact averaged cubic remainder. Retaining both ratios of its two oscillatory phases bounds the dual four-frequency multiplier by the reciprocal of the third largest frequency. A dyadic four-linear estimate sums this majorant without a logarithm and includes a mixed \(L^2\) endpoint. That endpoint controls the remainder at the numerical state without a numerical Sobolev bound. We then prove the full global estimate using the continuous trilinear bounds of Li and Wu, a stepwise residual calculation, low–high frequency stability, a restarted bootstrap, and density."

"In particular, the normal-form identity keeps both endpoints when the time interval is restarted, and its forcing term is estimated from the actual stepwise residual. A fixed-timestep approximation argument then removes the temporary smoothness used in the calculations."

The complete supplied proof, including all definitions, transformations, evolution equations, identities, estimates, experimental sections and bibliography, is retained in checked-source.md in original page order."}

The product containing \(f-w\) is bounded by \(\|f-w\|_2\|S_tF_n\|_\infty\le C_M\delta_n\) using the uniform \(H^1\) bound. Therefore
347: \[
348: \sup_{I_n}\|\partial_x^{-1}\mathcal B_t(f,F_n(t))\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n.
349: \]
350: 
351: <!-- PDF page 9 -->
352: 
353: Use (21) and \(Y_n'=\mathcal B_t(f,F_n)+\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(F_n,F_n)-\tau^{-1}W_n\) to get
354: \[
355: \sup_{I_n}\|\partial_x^{-1}Y_n\|_{L^2}\le C_M\tau q_n,\qquad
356: \sup_{I_n}\|\partial_x^{-1}Y_n'\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n. \tag{22}
357: \]
358: For the strong norm, (13) and \(F_n'=\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(f,f)\) give exactly
359: \[
360: C_n(t)=\tfrac13\mathcal J_t(f,F_n(t))-\tfrac16C_{[t_n,t]}(f,f,f).
361: \]
362: The first term is \(O(q_n)\) in \(L^2\). In the second, use (16) with exponent \(\gamma\) on \((w,w,w)\), and exponent zero on every term in the difference with \((f,f,f)\). Thus
363: \[
364: \sup_{I_n}\|Y_n\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n. \tag{23}
365: \]
366: Since \(p_*>1\), (22)–(23) imply the important pair
367: \[
368: \|Y_n\|_{X(I_n)}\le C_Mq_n,\qquad
369: \sup_{I_n}\|Y_n\|_{H^{-p_*}}\le C_M\tau q_n. \tag{24}
370: \]
371: 
372: **The residual**
373: 
374: Define on a step
375: \[
376: \rho_n(t)=-\int_{t_n}^t\mathcal B_s(Y_n,z_n)\,ds
377: -\tfrac12\int_{t_n}^t\mathcal B_s(Y_n,Y_n)\,ds
378: -\frac{t-t_n}{\tau}W_n.
379: \]
380: Concatenate these increments into \(\mathcal R(t)\), with \(\mathcal R(0)=0\). Then
381: \[
382: V'=\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(V,V)+\mathcal R',\qquad
383: \mathcal R'=-\mathcal B_t(Y_n,z_n)-\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(Y_n,Y_n)-\tau^{-1}W_n. \tag{25}
384: \]
385: We claim
386: \[
387: \sup_{I_n}\|\rho_n\|_{L^2}\le C_M\tau q_n,\qquad
388: \|\mathcal R'\|_{L^\infty(I_n;H^{-p_*})}\le C_Mq_n. \tag{26}
389: \]
390: For the first integral in \(\rho_n\), apply (13). The boundary term and the term containing \(Y_n'\) are each \(O(\tau q_n)\) by (22) and \(\|z_n\|_{L^2}\lesssim1\). Since \(z_n'=\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(f,f)\), the remaining term is a constant multiple of \(C(f,f,Y_n)\). In (15), put the negative norm on \(Y_n\) and use (24); the result is also \(O(\tau q_n)\). For the second integral apply (13) with \(Y_n\) in both slots. Its boundary and derivative terms are \(O(\tau q_n^2)=O(\tau q_n)\) because \(q_n\le2\). The \(W_n\) term is controlled by (21). This proves the first claim. The second follows directly from (25), (19), (21), and (23).
391: 
392: ### 4.4 Stability and completion of the proof
393: 
394: Set \(e=v-V\). On an interval \(I=[a,b]\) starting at a grid point, with \(h=b-a\le1\), let \(E_I=\sup_I\|e\|_{L^2}\) and assume \(E_I\le1\). The interval may end inside a step. The preceding bounds imply
395: \[
396: \sup_{a\le t\le b}\|\mathcal R(t)-\mathcal R(a)\|_{L^2}
397: \le C_M(h+\tau)(\tau^\gamma+E_I), \tag{27}
398: \]
399: \[
400: \|e\|_{X(I)}\le C_M(\tau^\gamma+E_I),\qquad
401: \|v\|_{X(I)}+\|V\|_{X(I)}\le C_M. \tag{28}
402: \]
403: Indeed \(e'=\mathcal B_t(e,v-e/2)-\mathcal R'\). There are at most \(h/\tau+1\) intersected steps, each starting with \(\delta_n\le E_I\), so (26) proves the first bound and the \(H^{-p_*}\) product estimate proves the second.
404: 
405: <!-- PDF page 10 -->
406: 
407: For any \(t\in I\), define \(\mathcal F_I(t)=\int_a^t\mathcal B_s(e,v-e/2)\,ds\). The exact error identity is
408: \[
409: e(t)=e(a)+\mathcal F_I(t)-(\mathcal R(t)-\mathcal R(a)). \tag{29}
410: \]
411: Choose a Fourier threshold \(N\ge2\) only in the proof. It is not part of the algorithm. The low frequencies satisfy
412: \[
413: \sup_{t\in I}\|P_{\le N}\mathcal F_I(t)\|_{L^2}\le C_MN^2hE_I. \tag{30}
414: \]
415: For example \(\|\partial_x^{-1}P(fg)\|_{L^2}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^2}\|g\|_{L^2}\), followed by the two-derivative Bernstein bound, proves (30).
416: 
417: For high frequencies, (13) gives, retaining *both* endpoints,
418: \[
419: \begin{aligned}
420: \mathcal F_I(t)
421: &=\tfrac13[\mathcal J_s(e,v-e/2)]_{s=a}^{s=t}
422: -\tfrac13C_{[a,t]}(e,v-e/2,V)-\tfrac16C_{[a,t]}(v,v,e)\\
423: &\quad+\tfrac13\int_a^t\mathcal J_s(\mathcal R',V)\,ds. \tag{31}
424: \end{aligned}
425: \]
426: For an explicit verification put \(g=v-e/2\). Then \(e'=\mathcal B(e,g)-\mathcal R'\) and \(g'=\tfrac12\mathcal B(v,v)-\tfrac12\mathcal B(e,g)+\tfrac12\mathcal R'\).
427: In the differentiated terms of (13), symmetry of \(\mathcal J\) gives \(C(e,g,g)-\tfrac12C(e,g,e)=C(e,g,V)\) because \(g-e/2=V\).
428: The remaining cubic term is \(\tfrac12C(v,v,e)\), and the forcing terms are
429: \(-\mathcal J(\mathcal R',g)+\tfrac12\mathcal J(e,\mathcal R')=-\mathcal J(\mathcal R',V)\).
430: Multiplication by \(-1/3\) yields exactly (31). The endpoint terms after \(P_{>N}\) are bounded by \(C_MN^{-1}E_I\) by the \(H^1\) bound for \(\mathcal J\) in (19).
431: 
432: We spell out how the high-output trilinear terms are estimated. If all three inputs have frequencies at most \(N/3\), the output cannot exceed \(N\). Write \(L=P_{\le N/3}\) and \(H=I-L\). The telescoping expansion is
433: \(C(f_1,f_2,f_3)-C(Lf_1,Lf_2,Lf_3)=C(Hf_1,f_2,f_3)+C(Lf_1,Hf_2,f_3)+C(Lf_1,Lf_2,Hf_3)\).
434: The low-input term has no output above \(N\), and each projection contracts both components of \(X(I)\). For the specified high input, \(\|Hf_i\|_{H^{-p_*}}\le CN^{-p_*}\|f_i\|_2\). In (15), place the \(H^{-p_*}\) norm on that input. Bernstein gives
435: \[
436: \|P_{>N}C_I(f_1,f_2,f_3)\|_{L^2}
437: \le Ch\prod_j\|f_j\|_{X(I)}+CN^{-p_*}\prod_j\|f_j\|_{L^\infty(I;L^2)}. \tag{32}
438: \]
439: Applying (28) to the middle two terms of (31) yields \(C_Mh\tau^\gamma+C_M(h+N^{-p_*})E_I\).
440: 
441: The last term of (31) requires the stepwise formula for \(\mathcal R'\) in (25). On each intersected step it becomes a sum of
442: \[
443: -C(Y_n,z_n,V),\qquad-\tfrac12C(Y_n,Y_n,V),\qquad
444: -\tau^{-1}\int\mathcal J_s(W_n,V)\,ds.
445: \]
446: The first two are \(O(\tau q_n)\) by (15), with the negative norm on \(Y_n\), and (24), (28). The last is \(O(\tau q_n)\) by (21) and the \(L^2\) bound for \(\mathcal J\). Even for a partial final step this is a valid upper bound. Summing gives \(C_M(h+\tau)(\tau^\gamma+E_I)\). Combining these facts,
447: \[
448: \sup_{t\in I}\|P_{>N}\mathcal F_I(t)\|_{L^2}
449: \le C_M(h+\tau)\tau^\gamma+C_M(h+\tau+N^{-1}+N^{-p_*})E_I. \tag{33}
450: \]
451: Equations (29), (27), (30), and (33) imply
452: \[
453: E_I\le\|e(a)\|_{L^2}+C_M(h+\tau)\tau^\gamma+
454: C_M(N^2h+h+\tau+N^{-1}+N^{-p_*})E_I. \tag{34}
455: \]
456: First fix \(N\) so large that \(C_M(N^{-1}+N^{-p_*})\le1/4\).
457: Next choose \(\delta\in(0,1]\) sufficiently small that \(C_M\delta(N^2+3)\le1/4\).
458: Restrict \(\tau\le\delta/2\). For intervals starting at grid points and having length at most \(\delta\), (34) gives
459: \[
460: E_I\le2\|e(a)\|_{L^2}+C_M'\delta\tau^\gamma. \tag{35}
461: \]
462: 
463: <!-- PDF page 11 -->
464: 
465: Use successive blocks of \(\lfloor\delta/\tau\rfloor\) steps, whose lengths lie in \([\delta/2,\delta]\), with a possibly shorter final block. The number of blocks is at most \(2T/\delta+1\), independently of \(\tau\). Iterating (35), starting with \(e(0)=0\), yields
466: \[
467: \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|e(t)\|_{L^2}\le C_{M,\gamma,T}\tau^\gamma, \tag{36}
468: \]
469: as long as the bootstrap bound is in force. By continuity, if \(\|e\|_{L^2}\) first reached one, the same block argument up to that time would give an upper bound \(C_{M,\gamma,T}\tau^\gamma\). Choosing \(\tau_0\) smaller so that this is less than \(1/2\) gives a contradiction. Hence (36) holds on all of \([0,T]\). The retained initial endpoint in (31) is estimated by \(E_I\) on each block, so the recurrence also applies when \(e(a)\ne0\).
470: 
471: For nonsmooth \(u_0\in H^\gamma\), approximate it by real, mean-zero trigonometric polynomials with uniformly bounded \(H^\gamma\) norm. Take \(u_{0,m}=P_{\le m}u_0\) so \(\|u_{0,m}\|_{H^\gamma}\le R\) and \(\|u_{0,m}-u_0\|_2\to0\).
472: Section 2.1 gives a common \(M\) and \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u_m-u\|_2\le C(T,2R)\|u_{0,m}-u_0\|_2\to0\).
473: For each fixed \(\tau\) and finite number of steps, the unmodified map (2) is continuous on \(L^2\): its factors contain inverse derivatives, and the \(H^1\) algebra estimate controls the products; factors such as \(\tau^{-1}\) are finite when \(\tau\) is fixed. Thus its iterates converge in \(L^2\). Indeed \(F_\tau:L^2\to H^1\) is a continuous quadratic map. The first term of \(H_\tau\) is a product of inverse derivatives; the second contains the continuous bilinear mean \(P_0(f^2)\); the third contains the \(H^1\) product \((S_sD^{-1}f)^3\) followed by \(D^{-1}\); and the fourth contains \(D^{-2}F_\tau(f)\) and \(D^{-1}f\), again \(H^1\) products followed by \(D^{-2}\). For fixed \(\tau>0\), all coefficients are finite. Every term is continuous from \(L^2\) to \(L^2\). Induction on the finite number \(L\) of steps gives \(u_m^n\to u^n\) at every grid point. Take the maximum over these \(L+1\) points and pass to the limit in (36); \(C,\tau_0\) are the same for all \(m\). The estimates never involved a higher Sobolev norm of the approximating data. Finally \(S_{t_n}\) is unitary and \(V(t_n)=S_{-t_n}u^n\), so the grid-point error is exactly \(\|u(t_n)-u^n\|_{L^2}\).
474: This proves Theorem 1."}

9: and [quantified implication](quantified-implication-example.md) examples.
10: These examples show format and derivations, not certified benchmark answers.
11: 
12: The complete [guarded-definition example](guarded-definition-example.md) shows
13: how to organize a target that includes an object's existence and a property
14: of that object. For a real a let Q(r) mean r=a. R001 first proves N001, unique
15: existence of a Q witness, without using w. D002 then defines w as that unique
16: witness with requires=[N001]. R002 takes N001 as a direct input and proves the

19: restricted domain when the frozen target requires a statement on the full
20: original domain. This pattern adds no new assumption or mathematical source.

22: ## Construct one coherent candidate
23: 
24: 1. For `target` and `definitions`, extract the original H, ambient parameters
25:    and global typed definitions. Preserve the original source locations. Do
26:    not change a parameter's mathematical kind while fixing its metadata.
27: 2. For N/R partitioning and `statement_closure`, follow the
28:    [NL0 constructor](../references/nl0_constructor.md). Build the actual nodes
29:    and complete exports under its LLM-task and qualitative-workload guidance.
30: 3. For `dependency_closure` and `argument`, construct
31:    each proof unit alongside its premises. List exact source inputs or display
32:    a prior local derivation for every substantive fact beyond the fixed
33:    calculations. Split when local context changes; avoid a giant S whose
34:    changing objects must later be repaired one at a time.
35: 4. For `sources` and `applicability`, inspect each selected native/primary
36:    source, preserve its complete contract and ground each instantiated premise.
37:    A signature lookup or a sentence claiming a hypothesis is true is not proof
38:    of that hypothesis. Reuse an adequate proved source rather than re-proving
39:    it; a project-specific bridge still requires its displayed derivation.
40: 5. For object declarations and local scopes under dependency_closure, introduce objects and conditional premises
41:    at their actual first use. Keep witness bases and local F dependencies
42:    correct. Preserve exact coefficients and ranges when copying calculations.
43: 6. Run check_draft, correct its actual located records, inspect every own
44:    conditional packet, and report readiness below. The independent auditor
45:    applies the same criteria after definitive submission.
46: 
47: ## Canonical data shapes
48: 
49: Submit {spec,graph} using the schema, or preserve an own draft with
50: {base_candidate:N,patches:[...]}. The controller binds identity, input/pin

56:

65: All ordinary validation and later Audit A still apply.
66: For reads only, an end beyond the string returns its remaining existing lines
67: and the actual range; the start must exist and at most 250 lines may be

70: Each D has type, full definition, binders, used objects, D dependencies and

72: and appropriate source/origin fields. Each R has direct inputs, one output,

102: ## Actual own-packet inspection and release
103: 
104: After structural validation call read_author_packet(candidate,inference) for
105: every R. The returned view contains the real direct input/output statements,

108: identify its actual input or previous derivation. Complete closing notes use
109: these existing evidence groups; their criterion IDs are supplied by the
110: controller from Audit A. Cite actual H/M/E/N/F/R/S or candidate locations in

116: {
117:   "candidate": 7,
118:   "readiness": "no_known_issue",

123:   "inference_notes": [{

125:     "dependency_and_local_assumption_check": "Actual factual grounds, calculation, compatible inputs and discharged assumptions, with locations.",
126:     "source_application_check": "Actual substitutions and grounds for every source premise, or why no source is used.",
127:     "declaration_check": "Actual object introductions, types, witness bases and scopes, with locations."

129: }

133: set readiness=unresolved and list an issue such as
134: {id:"I001",criterion:"dependency_closure",location:"/graph/inferences/0/argument/0/text",note:"The exact missing input/derivation."}.

140: inference notes check the exact source conclusion and any needed change of
141: domain or representation, rather than listing source names alone.
142: An empty new list cannot silently erase an old issue. The program checks
143: coverage, explicit state, locations and content/authority binding; mathematical
144: soundness still needs independent Audit A.
145: 
146: An actual own-packet read remains credited after an unrelated candidate edit
147: only when its complete displayed mathematical view and acceptance authority
148: have identical canonical contents. The recorded hash covers parameters, logic, selected
149: definitions, actual direct inputs/source contracts, output and full argument.
150: Changed views require new actual reads. Current whole-candidate release notes

153: 
154: Only author_release_ready allows complete-artifact submission. Otherwise
155: continue the actual local proof/source work in this same stage. At a real
156: budget limit preserve the draft as unfinished. Normal completion difficulties
157: are not a substantive mathematical-gap report. Source/graph edits invalidate
158: bound closing notes. When ready, resubmit the exact candidate. Fresh Audit A
159: receives none of these notes or historical feedback.

161: ## Library access
162: 
163: find_library_sources offers a small verified pinned metadata index, not a
164: whitelist. An exact canonical name selects that declaration; ordinary terms
165: return ranked candidates with actual matched terms. Overlap does not establish
166: applicability. probe_library resolves genuine aliases and the actual module;
167: its optional module argument is only a locator hint. Read the pinned source

169: application. Predicates/data definitions are not source theorems. Same-stage
170: M-label renumbering can reuse exact metadata through a disclosed mapping;
171: it does not rewrite any mathematical statement or applicability argument.
172: 
173: ## Background granularity
174: 
175: Follow Audit A's shared verified-background admission rule. Register the main
176: tools; write ordinary rigorous mathematics rather than anticipating every
177: small Lean lemma. Correct elementary compression is allowed. Audit A can
178: verify an omitted routine library fact and attach a note without an author
179: rewrite. Missing original H, source uncertainty and substantive proof gaps
180: remain blocking. These audit notes later accompany each Lean task."}

# Selected target: complete Theorem 1

Source: this run's original.pdf, Theorem 1 on page 2, with the standing conventions and solution class on pages 2–3. The entire source paper, including its supplied proof, is checked-source.md.

The time grid in scheme (2) is \(\tau=T/L\), \(t_n=n\tau\), with \(L\) a positive integer and \(n=0,\ldots,L\). The maximum in Theorem 1 is over all these grid points. For fixed \(T>0\), \(0<\gamma\le1\) and \(R>0\), its \(C,\tau_0>0\) depend only on \(T,\gamma,R\) and are uniform over the specified initial-data ball and all grids with \(\tau\le\tau_0\). The theorem is for the displayed time-semidiscrete update without a spatial cutoff.

The following is the complete source statement and its standing context, transcribed from pages 2–3.

## 2 The scheme and the main result

Use normalized measure \(dx/(2\pi)\) on \(\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\); changing to unnormalized \(L^2\) only changes constants. Write \(S_t=e^{-t\partial_x^3}\), so that \(\widehat{S_tf}(k)=e^{itk^3}\widehat f(k)\). Let \(P_0\) be the mean, \(P=I-P_0\), and define \(D^{-1}=\partial_x^{-1}\) with multiplier \((ik)^{-1}\) for \(k\ne0\) and zero at zero. Set \(D^{-2}=(D^{-1})^2\). Write
\[
\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
\|f\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\langle k\rangle^{2s}|\widehat f(k)|^2,
\qquad \langle k\rangle=(1+k^2)^{1/2}.
\]
Spaces are the completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms, with negative spaces interpreted as distributions. Orthogonality gives the normalized \(L^2\) identity for polynomials and hence for their completions. For mean-zero functions and \(s\ge0\), \(\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\le\|f\|_{H^s}\le2^{s/2}\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\); for \(s<0\), \(2^{s/2}\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\le\|f\|_{H^s}\le\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\). Real-valued means \(\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}\). All time suprema concern continuous representatives; derivative norms are essential suprema. The exact solution is the unique real mean-zero \(C([0,T];H^\gamma)\) solution obtained by smooth approximation, and satisfies the equation distributionally. The constants \(C_M\) may change from line to line and depend on \(\gamma,T,M\), but are uniform in \(n,\tau\) and spectral support.

The equation is
\[
u_t+u_{xxx}=\tfrac12\partial_x(u^2),\qquad u(0)=u_0. \tag{1}
\]
The fixed scheme is \(u^0=u_0\) and
\[
u^{n+1}=S_\tau u^n+F_\tau(u^n)+H_\tau(u^n),\qquad \tau=T/L, \tag{2}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_\tau(f)&=\tfrac16 P[(S_\tau D^{-1}f)^2]-\tfrac16 S_\tau P[(D^{-1}f)^2],\\
H_\tau(f)&=\tfrac13 P[(S_\tau D^{-1}f)D^{-1}F_\tau(f)]
+\tfrac{\tau}{9}(S_\tau D^{-1}f)P_0(f^2)\\
&\quad-\tfrac1{54}\left[S_{\tau-s}D^{-1}[(S_sD^{-1}f)^3]\right]_{s=0}^{s=\tau}\\
&\quad-\tfrac1{27\tau}\left[S_{\tau-s}D^{-2}[(S_{s-\tau}D^{-2}F_\tau(f))(S_sD^{-1}f)]\right]_{s=0}^{s=\tau}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the scheme of [1, Eq. (1.4)], without a spatial frequency cutoff.

**Theorem 1 (Logarithm-free convergence).** Let \(T>0\), \(0<\gamma\le1\), and \(R>0\). For real, mean-zero \(u_0\in H^\gamma(\mathbb T)\) with \(\|u_0\|_{H^\gamma}\le R\), there are \(C,\tau_0>0\), depending only on \(T,\gamma,R\), such that the scheme (2) satisfies
\[
\max_{0\le n\le L}\|u(n\tau)-u^n\|_{L^2}\le C\tau^\gamma
\qquad\text{whenever }\tau=T/L\le\tau_0.
\]

The periodic KdV bounds of Babin–Ilyin–Titi control the exact flow on the initial-data ball. The continuous estimates of [1, Proposition 3.4 and Lemma 7.2] will be used in the stability proof. The logarithmic convergence theorem itself is not used. For the exact twisted solution \(v(t)=S_{-t}u(t)\), set
\[
M=1+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|v(t)\|_{H^\gamma}.
\]
The source statements and the sign transformation giving a bound for \(M\) are recorded below in Section 2.1. No convergence theorem for the numerical scheme is used as an input. Intermediate constants may depend on \(M,\gamma,T\), but never on the timestep or a Fourier support bound.

<!-- PDF page 3 -->

### 2.1 The exact KdV flow

The source [2, Theorems 4.2–4.3, 5.1, 6.3–6.5] treats \(U_t=UU_x+U_{xxx}\) on the same torus, with normalized measure and mean-zero homogeneous Sobolev norms. Theorem 4.2 bounds its Galerkin flows on \([0,T]\) in \(\dot H^s\) by a constant depending only on \(s,T,\|U_0\|_{\dot H^s}\) and an upper bound for \(\|U_0\|_2\). Theorem 4.3 gives a distributional limiting solution with the same bound. Theorems 5.1 (\(s>1/2\)) and 6.3 (\(0<s\le1/2\)) give its uniqueness, \(C([0,T];\dot H^s)\) regularity and continuous dependence. Theorem 6.4 covers \(s=0\), and Theorem 6.5 with \(\theta=0\) states that, for two flows whose initial \(L^2\) norms sum to at most \(B\),
\(\sup_{[0,T]}\|U-\widetilde U\|_2\le C(T,B)\|U_0-\widetilde U_0\|_2\).
Together these results specify the continuous flow and the uniform bounds needed here.

Define \(u(t,x)=-U(t,-x)\). Then \(u_t=-U_t\), \(u_x=U_x\), \(u_{xxx}=U_{xxx}\) at \((t,-x)\), and consequently \(u_t+u_{xxx}=uu_x\). Fourier coefficients become \(\widehat u(k)=-\widehat U(-k)\), preserving every Sobolev norm, reality and zero mean. This transforms the source equation to (1). The norm comparison above transfers all bounds to our \(H^\gamma\) norm. Hence there is \(A(T,\gamma,R)<\infty\) such that every smooth initial datum in the stated ball satisfies \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u(t)\|_{H^\gamma}\le A\). The same bound holds for the limiting solution: for each finite set of frequencies pass to the limit in its finite norm sum, then take the supremum over finite sets. Thus \(M\le1+A(T,\gamma,R)\) uniformly. Continuous dependence in \(L^2\) is precisely the input used in the final density passage. No change of torus length or amplitude scaling is needed.


## Supplied proof route

The following sentences are transcribed from the supplied paper's abstract/introduction:

"The main estimate concerns the exact averaged cubic remainder. Retaining both ratios of its two oscillatory phases bounds the dual four-frequency multiplier by the reciprocal of the third largest frequency. A dyadic four-linear estimate sums this majorant without a logarithm and includes a mixed \(L^2\) endpoint. That endpoint controls the remainder at the numerical state without a numerical Sobolev bound. We then prove the full global estimate using the continuous trilinear bounds of Li and Wu, a stepwise residual calculation, low–high frequency stability, a restarted bootstrap, and density."

"In particular, the normal-form identity keeps both endpoints when the time interval is restarted, and its forcing term is estimated from the actual stepwise residual. A fixed-timestep approximation argument then removes the temporary smoothness used in the calculations."

The complete supplied proof, including all definitions, transformations, evolution equations, identities, estimates, experimental sections and bibliography, is retained in checked-source.md in original page order.
spec.conclusion: There exist C>0 and tau0>0, depending only on T,gamma,R and valid simultaneously on the whole stated initial-data ball, such that for every real mean-zero g in H^gamma(torus) with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0, the exact solution u_g (the unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) distributional KdV solution obtained by smooth approximation) and the unfiltered scheme u_g^0=g, u_g^{n+1}=Psi_tau(u_g^n) satisfy max_{0<=n<=L}||u_g(n tau)-u_g^n||_{L2}<=C tau^gamma. In particular this holds for the supplied u0, including n=0, without any spatial frequency cutoff.

propositions.statement: There is a finite A(T,gamma,R) uniform for every real mean-zero datum g with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R. Its KdV equation u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2), u(0)=g, has a unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) solution obtained by smooth approximation, solving the equation distributionally, with sup_t||u(t)||_{H^gamma}<=A. Smooth data give spatially smooth solutions. For v(t)=S_{-t}u(t), v'=B_t(v,v)/2 and all Sobolev norms of v and u agree. For two such exact flows with initial L2 norms summing to at most B0, sup_t||u-tilde u||_2<=C(T,B0)||g-tilde g||_2. In particular M=1+sup_t||v(t)||_{H^gamma}<=1+A uniformly.

argument.text: H001 supplies the positive horizon and 0<gamma<=1. Apply E001 with s=gamma, horizon T, initial L2 bound R and initial dot H^gamma bound R, to arbitrary real mean-zero data in that ball. The source has normalized measure. It gives a bound uniform over these bounded norms and a solution. Its uniqueness/continuity branch is 5.1 for gamma>1/2 and 6.3 for 0<gamma<=1/2. The source theta=0 estimate gives uniform L2 dependence with initial sum bound B0. These applications concern only exact flows, not scheme convergence.

argument.text: Define \(u(t,x)=-U(t,-x)\). Then \(u_t=-U_t\), \(u_x=U_x\), \(u_{xxx}=U_{xxx}\) at \((t,-x)\), and consequently \(u_t+u_{xxx}=uu_x\). Fourier coefficients become \(\widehat u(k)=-\widehat U(-k)\), preserving every Sobolev norm, reality and zero mean. This transforms the source equation to (1). The norm comparison above transfers all bounds to our \(H^\gamma\) norm. Hence there is \(A(T,\gamma,R)<\infty\) such that every smooth initial datum in the stated ball satisfies \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u(t)\|_{H^\gamma}\le A\). The same bound holds for the limiting solution: for each finite set of frequencies pass to the limit in its finite norm sum, then take the supremum over finite sets. Thus \(M\le1+A(T,\gamma,R)\) uniformly. Continuous dependence in \(L^2\) is precisely the input used in the final density passage. No change of torus length or amplitude scaling is needed. More explicitly, the physical change u(t,x)=-U(t,-x) maps initial data g to source initial data -g(-x), so preserves the whole initial-data ball. The homogeneous-to-inhomogeneous inequalities follow coefficientwise from |k|<=<k><=sqrt(2)|k| for k!=0. For a continuous limiting flow the finite-frequency sums and then their supremum give the bound at each time, with the same constant. Apply the source pair bound after this isometry; it gives the stated C(T,B0) bound. Twisting by S_{-t} differentiates away -partial_x^3 and gives v'=B_t(v,v)/2. This proves all clauses of N001, for arbitrary data in the ball.

argument.text:
Fix tau>0 and real phases alpha,beta. Also, independently, fix a nonzero integer quadruple of zero sum. Assume L1 to collect these antecedent conditions. If either phase vanishes its covariance vanishes by its definition. For the remaining phase case use the following calculation.
 Let \(h(s)=e^{-i\alpha s}-M_\tau(e^{-i\alpha s})\). Then \(\eta_\tau=\tau^{-1}\int_0^\tau h(s)e^{-i\beta s}\,ds\). The elementary bound
\(|h(s)|\le\tau^{-1}\int_0^\tau|\alpha||s-r|\,dr\le\tau|\alpha|\)
gives the linear phase bound in N002, also interchanging \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Moreover,
\[
|h(0)|+|h(\tau)|\le\tau|\alpha|,\qquad
\int_0^\tau|h'(s)|\,ds=\tau|\alpha|.
\]
Integrating \(e^{-i\beta s}\) once gives \(|\eta_\tau|\le2|\alpha/\beta|\). Interchanging the phases proves the ratio bound in N002.

argument.text:
For the quadruple let A=|ab|, B0=|cd| and N1>=N2>=N3>=N4 be the sorted magnitudes. The largest magnitude is at most the sum of the other three, hence N1<=3N2.
 For the required ratio majorant, if \(d\) is among the two largest frequencies, use \(\min(A/B0,B0/A)\le1\). Otherwise the largest two are among \(a,b,c\). If they are \(a,b\), then
\[
\frac1{|d|}\min(A/B0,B0/A)\le\frac{|c|}{|ab|}\le\frac1{N_3}.
\]
If they are \(a,c\) (the case \(b,c\) is identical), their ratio is between \(1/3\) and \(3\). The remaining magnitudes are \(|b|,|d|\), whose maximum is \(N_3\). Thus
\[
\frac1{|d|}\min(A/B0,B0/A)\le3\min\left\{\frac{|b|}{|d|^2},\frac1{|b|}\right\}
\le\frac3{\max(|b|,|d|)}.
\]
For the required sum majorant, consider the pairing \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\). If the two largest magnitudes are in the same pair, the other pair has sum of magnitude at most \(2N_3\). Since \(a+b=-(c+d)\),
\[
\frac{|a+b|}{\max(A,B0)}\le\frac{2N_3}{N_1N_2}\le\frac2{N_3}.
\]
If the largest two belong to different pairs, the third largest is paired with one of them. Hence \(\max(A,B0)\ge N_2N_3\) and \(|a+b|\le2N_1\le6N_2\), giving the result. Ties can be ordered arbitrarily; the same alternatives cover them. 
This covers all placements and ties. Discharge L1 and universally quantify both independent choices to obtain N002.

argument.text:
Fix four nonnegative ell2 sequences, under temporary antecedent L1.  It suffices first to consider finitely supported sequences. Decompose into shells \(2^j\le|k|<2^{j+1}\), \(j\ge0\), and write \(Xshell_{r,j}\) for the \(\ell^2\) norm of the \(r\)th sequence on the \(j\)th shell. Fix an ordering of the four shell indices \(j_1\ge j_2\ge j_3\ge j_4\). A nonzero zero-sum interaction has \(j_1-j_2\le2\). For each fixed pair of smaller-shell frequencies, the remaining sum of the two larger-shell sequences is at most their \(\ell^2\) norm product by Cauchy–Schwarz, since one sequence is a translated reflection of the other. Sum the smaller frequencies in \(\ell^1\). A shell has at most \(2^{j+1}\) integer elements, so another Cauchy–Schwarz bound gives
\[
\sum_{a+b+c+d=0}\prod_{r=1}^4 x_{r,j_r}
\le C2^{(j_3+j_4)/2}\prod_{r=1}^4 Xshell_{r,j_r}.
\]
Since \(N_3\ge2^{j_3}\), the weight leaves \(C2^{-(j_3-j_4)/2}\). For \(q=j_1-j_2\in\{0,1,2\}\), extend the nonnegative sum by dropping the upper restriction on the smaller shells. The contribution is at most
\[
C\left(\sum_{J0} Xshell_{1,J0}Xshell_{2,J0-q}\right)
\left(\sum_{\ell\ge m}2^{-(\ell-m)/2}Xshell_{3,\ell}Xshell_{4,m}\right).
\]
The first factor is bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz. Writing \(r=\ell-m\), the second is at most
\[
\sum_{r\ge0}2^{-r/2}\|Xshell_3\|_{\ell^2}\|Xshell_4\|_{\ell^2}
=\frac{\|Xshell_3\|_{\ell^2}\|Xshell_4\|_{\ell^2}}{1-2^{-1/2}}.
\]
Sum over at most 24 orderings and three offsets. For arbitrary nonnegative sequences apply the finite bound to their restrictions to \(|k|\le m\). The infinite positive sum is the supremum of these finite sums, while the norms of the restrictions are bounded by the full norms. This proves the infinite statement without exchanging conditionally convergent sums. 
Restriction to a subset only decreases the nonnegative sum. Discharge L1 to obtain the universally quantified N003.

argument.text:
H001 supplies 0<gamma<=1 for the final numerical-state specialization. Independently fix lambda in [0,1], tau>0, step time t_n, and mean-zero polynomial inputs. Temporarily assume these range conditions as L1. Use the following computation with the proof's letter gamma replaced everywhere by lambda; no numerical state regularity is assumed.
 Only nonzero \(abck\) and \(p=a+b\ne0\) need consideration. Set \(d=-k\). N002 and the first majorant in N002 give
\[
\frac{|\eta|}{|k|}\le\frac6{N_3}.
\]
For the other endpoint, observe that \(AB=|abck|\), and use the linear phase bound in N002 and the second majorant in N002:
\[
\frac{|\eta|}{\tau|abck|}\le3\frac{|p|\min(A,B)}{AB}
=3\frac{|p|}{\max(A,B)}\le\frac{18}{N_3}.
\]
Taking the geometric mean of these two bounds yields
\[
\boxed{\frac{|\eta_\tau(\alpha,\beta)|}{|k||abc|^\lambda}
\le\frac{6^{1-\lambda}18^\lambda\tau^\lambda}{N_3(a,b,c,-k)}.} 
\]



Dualize the remainder definition D014 against an \(\ell^2\) sequence and take absolute values. Apply N003 with \(x_1(a)=|a|^\lambda|\widehat f_1(a)|\) and analogously for \(x_2,x_3\); \(x_4(d)\) is the absolute value of the dual coefficient at \(-d\). Their norms are bounded by the inhomogeneous Sobolev norms and the dual norm. The factors \(e^{-it_n\Phi}\) have modulus one. This proves the theorem, including the assertion about restricted sums. Polynomial approximation and the bound extend the operator to the claimed spaces. 
Here the two estimates used are directly N002 and the four-linear estimate is N003. At lambda=0 or 1 use the corresponding endpoint directly, so no 0^0 convention is needed.

argument.text:
The polynomial estimate F001 makes each Cauchy approximation converge in L2: expand a trilinear difference into three terms and apply the same bound. It gives a unique continuous trilinear extension to the mean-zero H^lambda completions and preserves the multiplier restrictions. For the numerical-state estimate fix mean-zero w in H^gamma, f in L2, ||w||_{H^gamma}<=M, delta=||f-w||_2<=1, and 0<tau<=1.  Apply F001 at lambda=gamma with exponent \(\gamma\) to \((w,w,w)\). Expand the difference between the cubic expressions at \(f\) and at \(w\), and apply F001 at lambda=0 to every difference term. This gives \(C\tau\delta(\|f\|_{L^2}+\|w\|_{L^2})^2\). No \(H^\gamma\) bound on the numerical state is used. 
Indeed ||f||_2<=M+1, so the difference is bounded by C_M tau delta, while the value at w is <=C M^3 tau^(1+gamma). These establish both assertions. Discharge L1 and the stated conditional specialization, retaining all its conditions in the output.

argument.text: Use H001. For E002 take arbitrary I=[a,b] subset [0,T] with b-a<=1 and lambda=0 for the X estimate. X gives precisely L-infinity L2 and L-infinity H^(-23/14) derivative, its hypotheses. Its three choices of negative-norm slot are retained. For constant inputs use E002 with any lambda in [0,1]. Each source spatial norm is sqrt(2 pi) times ours: divide by sqrt(2 pi) on the output and absorb the remaining product factors 2 pi into the constant. This proves the first two assertions without changing their exponent or time length. Smooth or continuous piecewise smooth time functions have the stated distributional derivative, so E002 applies directly. General X inputs use the source bounded interpretation of the operator.

argument.text:
For the product and stages use E003 with lambda=gamma and epsilon=1/8 at gamma=1/2. The diagonal bilinear stage is exactly F_n(t;w), by definition. The necessary source exponent checks and retained calculations are:
when \(\|w\|_{H^\gamma}\le M\). One can take \(a_\gamma=1/2-\gamma\) for \(0<\gamma<1/2\), \(1/8\) for \(\gamma=1/2\), and \(a_\gamma=0\) for \(\gamma>1/2\). For clarity, the source stage exponent is \(\theta=(1+\gamma-\beta)/(1+\gamma-\beta_0)\), with \(\beta_0=2\gamma-3/2\) for \(0<\gamma<1/2\), \(\beta_0=-1/2-\epsilon\) for \(\gamma=1/2\), and \(\beta_0=\gamma-1\) for \(1/2<\gamma\le1\). Take \(\epsilon=1/8\) in the middle case. At \(\beta=a_\gamma\) the exponents are respectively \((1/2+2\gamma)/(5/2-\gamma)\ge\gamma\), \(11/17>1/2\) and \((1+\gamma)/2\ge\gamma\). Every \(a_\gamma\) lies in the source interval \([\beta_0,1+\gamma]\). Since \(0<\tau\le1\), these exponents imply the first bound in the asserted stage inequalities. At \(\beta=1+\gamma\) the exponent is zero, giving the second. Inequality the asserted product inequality is the source E003, with the same fixed \(1/8\) choice when \(\gamma=1/2\). Source \(L^2\) and \(H^s\) norms are \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) times ours; dividing the source inequalities absorbs only fixed factors into constants. These estimates require no regularity beyond \(H^\gamma\) on \(w\). Finally the elementary one-dimensional bounds are
For the first range the exponent inequality reduces to gamma^2-gamma/2+1/2=(gamma-1/4)^2+7/16>0; at gamma=1/2 the exponent is 11/17 and in the last range (1+gamma)/2>=gamma. Thus both stage conclusions follow uniformly for 0<tau<=1. All relevant bounds and the product inequality have now been proved in the declared normalization.

argument.text: Fix functions in the classes stated in the output; retain those conditions as L1. Orthogonality of finite Fourier polynomials gives Parseval, hence the completion identifies H^0 with normalized L2. The multiplier exp(itk^3) has modulus one, so S_t is an isometry. Its conjugate relation at -k proves preservation of reality, and its zero coefficient proves preservation of the mean. Every Fourier projection deletes nonnegative terms of squared Sobolev sums and commutes with time derivatives, so contracts Sobolev norms and both terms of X. Comparing <k> powers on |k|<=N and |k|>N gives the two stated Bernstein inequalities, with fixed constants for N>=1. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ||Dinv f||_infinity<=(sum_{k!=0}k^(-2))^(1/2)||f||_2 and ||Dinv f||_{H^1}<=sqrt(2)||f||_2. The analogous Fourier estimate gives ||A0||_infinity<=C||A0||_{H^1}. The product rule, placing the undifferentiated factor in L-infinity in each term, gives ||A0 B0||_{H^1}<=C||A0||_{H^1}||B0||_{H^1}. Thus J_t has the asserted H^1 bound. Also ||J_t(f,g)||_2<=||S_t Dinv f||_2||S_t Dinv g||_infinity<=C||Dinv f||_2||g||_2. Density extends these products from polynomials.

produces.statement: S_t, the Fourier projections, the inverse derivative and H^1 products satisfy the asserted isometry, projection, Bernstein, inverse-derivative and J estimates.

argument.text: For L2 F,G the convolution coefficient bound |(FG)hat(k)|<=||F||_2||G||_2 follows by Cauchy–Schwarz. Hence ||B_t(f,g)||_{H^(-pstar)}^2<=||f||_2^2||g||_2^2 sum_{k!=0}k^2<k>^(-2pstar). This series is finite because pstar=23/14>3/2. The same coefficient bound with sum_{k!=0}k^(-2) yields ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2. For mean-zero A, <k>^(-pstar)<=|k|^(-1) for k!=0 because pstar>1, giving its claimed negative-norm inequality. All constants are independent of time by F001.

produces.statement: The asserted B negative-norm bound, Dinv P product bound and negative-norm comparison hold.

argument.text: For smooth mean-zero time-dependent f,g, J_t(f,g) has coefficient sum_{a0+b0=k} exp(-3itka0b0)(ia0)^(-1)(ib0)^(-1) fhat(a0)ghat(b0) at k!=0. Differentiate: the phase derivative is 3ik times the product coefficient, so partial_t J_t(f,g)=3 B_t(f,g)+J_t(f',g)+J_t(f,g'). Integrating proves the stated normal form, retaining both endpoints. The sums of smooth functions and all needed derivatives converge absolutely, justifying differentiation and integration. Symmetry is immediate from the product. Since Dinv partial_x=P, substitution gives J_t(B_t(f,g),h)=S_{-t}P{P[(S_tf)(S_tg)]S_t Dinv h}; integrate to get C_I. For a continuous piecewise smooth pair, apply on each piece; adjacent boundary values cancel, leaving both outer endpoints. No delta mass appears in its distributional derivative. Discharge L1, retaining each specified function class in its universally quantified clause.

argument.text: Assume L1: the current datum u0 is smooth real and mean-zero, and let L be an arbitrary positive integer. Fix a smooth real mean-zero initial datum and an arbitrary positive integer L. H001 makes tau=T/L>0. The update preserves smoothness by its products, inverse derivatives and Airy multipliers. Its first and all projected terms have mean zero; the mean of the second H_tau term vanishes because S_tau Dinv f has mean zero. Conjugate symmetry is preserved by real products, real differential operators and the Airy group, so the iterates are real. Induction establishes these properties at every grid point. E004 applied at each f=v^n gives exactly v^{n+1}=f+F_n(t_{n+1})+C_n(t_{n+1})-R2(f,f,f). In V the Q_n endpoint and its occurrence in W_n cancel. Thus V(t_n)=f and V(t_{n+1})=v^{n+1}, proving continuity between steps. Differentiating its smooth step integrals gives F_n'=B_t(f,f)/2 and V'=B_t(f+F_n,f+F_n)/2-W_n/tau. Subtract F_n' to get the claimed Y_n' and note Y_n(t_n)=0. The construction is spatially smooth and piecewise time-smooth, as claimed. Discharge L1, keeping smoothness and the real mean-zero conditions in the conditional universally quantified output.

argument.text:
Fix arbitrary smooth mean-zero f,w on the step, and assume L1: t_n>=0, 0<tau<=1, ||w||_{H^gamma}<=M and delta_n=||f-w||_2<=1. Set q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n; thus q_n<=2 and ||f||_2<=M+1. H001 fixes the exponent range. N006 gives the endpoint normal form and product bounds; N005 gives product and exact-data stage bounds; N004 gives the numerical-state cubic bound. In the following calculations F001 denotes the collection proved in this paragraph, so occurrences of that label refer to the individual bounds just established, rather than an extra premise.
The endpoint formula \(F_n(t)=\tfrac16[\mathcal J_s(f,f)]_{t_n}^t\) gives
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|F_n(t)\|_{H^1}\le C_M,\qquad
\sup_{I_n}\|F_n(t)-F_n(t;w)\|_{H^1}\le C_M\delta_n.
\]
Together with the stage bounds N005, this yields
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|F_n(t)\|_{H^{a_\gamma}}+\sup_{I_n}\|F_n(t)\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n,
\qquad\|z_n\|_{X(I_n)}\le C_M. 
\]
For the exact-data contribution, apply the product bound N005 to \(\partial_x(S_tF_n(t;w))\) and \(S_tF_n(t;w)\); use the stage bounds N005. Write \(A=F_n(t;w)\) and \(D=F_n(t)-A\). The exact-data term obeys
\(\|\partial_x[(S_tA)^2]\|_2\le2C_\gamma\|A\|_{H^{1+\gamma}}\|A\|_{H^{a_\gamma}}\le C_M\tau^\gamma\).
The difference of squares is \((S_tD)S_t(F_n+A)\); both second factors have bounded \(H^1\) norm and \(\|D\|_{H^1}\le C_M\delta_n\). The \(H^1\) algebra estimate bounds its derivative by \(C_M\delta_n\). Thus
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|\mathcal B_t(F_n(t),F_n(t))\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n.
\]
Consequently N004 implies
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|Q_n(t)\|_{L^2}+\|W_n\|_{L^2}\le C_M\tau q_n. 
These are all asserted stage and endpoint-correction bounds.

produces.statement: Uniformly on I_n, ||F_n||_H^1<=C_M, ||F_n-F_n(.;w)||_H^1<=C_M delta_n, ||F_n||_H^{a_gamma}+||F_n||_2<=C_M q_n, ||z_n||_X<=C_M, ||B_t(F_n,F_n)||_2<=C_M q_n and sup||Q_n||_2+||W_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n.

argument.text:
To bound \(D^{-1}\mathcal B_t(f,F_n)\), use its exact expression \(S_{-t}P[(S_tf)(S_tF_n)]\). The product containing \(w\) is bounded by \(C_\gamma\|w\|_{H^\gamma}\|F_n\|_{H^{a_\gamma}}\). The product containing \(f-w\) is bounded by \(\|f-w\|_2\|S_tF_n\|_\infty\le C_M\delta_n\) using the uniform \(H^1\) bound. Therefore
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|\partial_x^{-1}\mathcal B_t(f,F_n(t))\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n.
\]



Use F001 and \(Y_n'=\mathcal B_t(f,F_n)+\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(F_n,F_n)-\tau^{-1}W_n\) to get
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|\partial_x^{-1}Y_n\|_{L^2}\le C_M\tau q_n,\qquad
\sup_{I_n}\|\partial_x^{-1}Y_n'\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n. 
\]
For the strong norm, the normal-form identity N006 and \(F_n'=\tfrac12\mathcal B_t(f,f)\) give exactly
\[
C_n(t)=\tfrac13\mathcal J_t(f,F_n(t))-\tfrac16C_{[t_n,t]}(f,f,f).
\]
The first term is \(O(q_n)\) in \(L^2\). In the second, use the constant-input trilinear bound N005 with exponent \(\gamma\) on \((w,w,w)\), and exponent zero on every term in the difference with \((f,f,f)\). Thus
\[
\sup_{I_n}\|Y_n\|_{L^2}\le C_Mq_n. 
\]
Since \(p_*>1\), the defect bounds just calculated–the defect bounds just calculated imply the important pair
\[
\|Y_n\|_{X(I_n)}\le C_Mq_n,\qquad
\sup_{I_n}\|Y_n\|_{H^{-p_*}}\le C_M\tau q_n. 
\]
For the first term in the exact formula for C_n, use the symmetric asymmetric J bound of N006 with ||F_n||_2<=C_M q_n from F001. Time-independent C_I terms use N005 on (w,w,w) at gamma and on every multilinear difference term at zero. The H^(-pstar) and derivative conclusions follow coefficientwise from Dinv and pstar>1, as in N006. This proves all clauses of N008. Discharge L1 and quantify the choices; each condition remains in the antecedent.

argument.text: Work with the smooth trajectory N007. Assume L1: the step comparison conditions of N009. Put w=v(t_n), f=v^n, delta_n=||f-w||_2 and q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n<=2. H001 fixes the exponent. The definition of Res concatenates increments rho_n with rho_n(t_n)=0; thus Res is continuous piecewise smooth with Res(0)=0. N007 gives V'=B_t(z_n,z_n)/2-W_n/tau. Expanding V=z_n+Y_n proves V'=B_t(V,V)/2+Res', with Res'=-B_t(Y_n,z_n)-B_t(Y_n,Y_n)/2-W_n/tau.

produces.statement: The exact residual identities in N009 hold, with Res continuous and piecewise smooth.

argument.text: Apply the N006 normal form to the first integral in rho_n. Since Y_n(t_n)=0, its endpoint bound is C||Dinv Y_n||_2||z_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n by N008. The derivative integral with Y_n' is <=C tau sup||Dinv Y_n'||_2 sup||z_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n. Since z_n'=B_t(f,f)/2, the other derivative term is a constant times C_[t_n,t](f,f,Y_n); N005 with negative norm on Y_n bounds it by C_M tau q_n using both ||Y_n||_X<=C_M q_n and ||Y_n||_H^(-pstar)<=C_M tau q_n. Apply N006 again to the integral with two Y_n slots. Its endpoint and derivative terms are each O(tau q_n^2), by N008, and q_n<=2 makes this O(tau q_n). The affine W_n term is <=||W_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n. This proves sup||rho_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n at every partial endpoint. Finally F001 and the B bound N006 give ||Res'||_H^(-pstar)<=C_M(q_n+q_n^2)+||W_n||_2/tau<=C_M q_n. Discharge L1 to obtain the conditional bounds, together with the unconditional residual identities, in N009.

argument.text: Use H001 and a smooth datum in the ball. N001 gives its smooth exact twisted flow v and M. N007 gives continuous V agreeing with the numerical grid. Put e=v-V, I=[a,b], h=b-a<=1, starting at a grid point. Assume L1: 0<tau<=1 and E_I=sup_I||e||_2<=1. Every intersected step has delta_n=||e(t_n)||_2<=E_I. Summing the N009 increment bound over at most h/tau+1 steps gives sup_I||Res(t)-Res(a)||_2<=C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I). The exact derivative identity is e'=B_t(e,v-e/2)-Res'. Apply N006 and N009 to get ||e||_X<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I). Also ||V||_2<=||v||_2+1 and V'=B(V,V)/2+Res' give ||v||_X+||V||_X<=C_M. Continuity permits these statements across step interfaces.

produces.statement: On I, sup||Res(t)-Res(a)||_2<=C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I), ||e||_X<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I), ||v||_X+||V||_X<=C_M, and e'=B_t(e,v-e/2)-Res'.

argument.text:
For any \(t\in I\), define \(\mathcal F_I(t)=\int_a^t\mathcal B_s(e,v-e/2)\,ds\). The exact error identity is
\[
e(t)=e(a)+\mathcal F_I(t)-(\mathcal R(t)-\mathcal R(a)). 
\]
Choose a Fourier threshold \(N\ge2\) only in the proof. It is not part of the algorithm. The low frequencies satisfy
\[
\sup_{t\in I}\|P_{\le N}\mathcal F_I(t)\|_{L^2}\le C_MN^2hE_I. 
\]
For example \(\|\partial_x^{-1}P(fg)\|_{L^2}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^2}\|g\|_{L^2}\), followed by the two-derivative Bernstein bound, proves the error identity.

For high frequencies, the normal-form identity N006 gives, retaining *both* endpoints,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F_I(t)
&=\tfrac13[\mathcal J_s(e,v-e/2)]_{s=a}^{s=t}
-\tfrac13C_{[a,t]}(e,v-e/2,V)-\tfrac16C_{[a,t]}(v,v,e)\\
&\quad+\tfrac13\int_a^t\mathcal J_s(\mathcal R',V)\,ds. 
\end{aligned}
\]
For an explicit verification put \(g=v-e/2\). Then \(e'=\mathcal B(e,g)-\mathcal R'\) and \(g'=\tfrac12\mathcal B(v,v)-\tfrac12\mathcal B(e,g)+\tfrac12\mathcal R'\).
In the differentiated terms of the normal-form identity N006, symmetry of \(\mathcal J\) gives \(C(e,g,g)-\tfrac12C(e,g,e)=C(e,g,V)\) because \(g-e/2=V\).
The remaining cubic term is \(\tfrac12C(v,v,e)\), and the forcing terms are
\(-\mathcal J(\mathcal R',g)+\tfrac12\mathcal J(e,\mathcal R')=-\mathcal J(\mathcal R',V)\).
Multiplication by \(-1/3\) yields exactly the normal-form expansion. The endpoint terms after \(P_{>N}\) are bounded by \(C_MN^{-1}E_I\) by the \(H^1\) bound for \(\mathcal J\) in the elementary bounds N006.
Here P_{<=N} denotes the multiplier 1_{|k|<=N}; its complement is P_{>N}. The low estimate uses N006's Dinv P product bound and the factor k^2<=N^2. F001 gives the differentiated equations, and N006 justifies the normal form piecewise: continuous interface endpoints cancel. The initial endpoint at a is retained even when e(a)!=0.

produces.statement: With mathcal F_I(t)=integral_a^t B_s(e,v-e/2)ds, e(t)=e(a)+mathcal F_I(t)-(Res(t)-Res(a)) and sup||P_{<=N}mathcal F_I||_2<=C_M N^2 h E_I. Exactly mathcal F_I(t)=(1/3)[J_s(e,v-e/2)]_a^t-(1/3)C_[a,t](e,v-e/2,V)-(1/6)C_[a,t](v,v,e)+(1/3)integral_a^t J_s(Res',V)ds. The high-output boundary terms are <=C_M N^(-1)E_I.

argument.text:
We spell out how the high-output trilinear terms are estimated. If all three inputs have frequencies at most \(N/3\), the output cannot exceed \(N\). Write \(Lo=P_{\le N/3}\) and \(Hi=I-Lo\). The telescoping expansion is
\(C(f_1,f_2,f_3)-C(Lof_1,Lof_2,Lof_3)=C(Hif_1,f_2,f_3)+C(Lof_1,Hif_2,f_3)+C(Lof_1,Lof_2,Hif_3)\).
The low-input term has no output above \(N\), and each projection contracts both components of \(X(I)\). For the specified high input, \(\|Hif_i\|_{H^{-p_*}}\le CN^{-p_*}\|f_i\|_2\). In the time-dependent trilinear bound N005, place the \(H^{-p_*}\) norm on that input. Bernstein gives
\[
\|P_{>N}C_I(f_1,f_2,f_3)\|_{L^2}
\le Ch\prod_j\|f_j\|_{X(I)}+CN^{-p_*}\prod_j\|f_j\|_{L^\infty(I;L^2)}. 
\]
Applying F001 to the middle two terms of the high-output trilinear estimate just derived yields \(C_Mh\tau^\gamma+C_M(h+N^{-p_*})E_I\).

The last term of the high-output trilinear estimate just derived requires the stepwise formula for \(\mathcal R'\) in the residual identity N009. On each intersected step it becomes a sum of
\[
-C(Y_n,z_n,V),\qquad-\tfrac12C(Y_n,Y_n,V),\qquad
-\tau^{-1}\int\mathcal J_s(W_n,V)\,ds.
\]
The first two are \(O(\tau q_n)\) by the time-dependent trilinear bound N005, with the negative norm on \(Y_n\), and F002, F001. The last is \(O(\tau q_n)\) by F001 and the \(L^2\) bound for \(\mathcal J\). Even for a partial final step this is a valid upper bound. Summing gives \(C_M(h+\tau)(\tau^\gamma+E_I)\). Combining these facts,
\[
\sup_{t\in I}\|P_{>N}\mathcal F_I(t)\|_{L^2}
\le C_M(h+\tau)\tau^\gamma+C_M(h+\tau+N^{-1}+N^{-p_*})E_I. 
\]
The projection names here are Lo=P_{<=N/3} and Hi=I-Lo. By N006 they commute with time derivatives and contract X. The middle two normal-form terms each contain e once, hence their products of L2 norms contribute E_I and products of X norms contribute tau^gamma+E_I, by F001. N005 applies with any selected high input in its negative-norm slot. In the forcing integrals use the stepwise identity N009, the two Y_n norms in N008 and the bounds on V in F001. The O(tau q_n) sum includes a possible partial last step.

produces.statement: sup_{t in I}||P_{>N}mathcal F_I(t)||_2<=C_M(h+tau)tau^gamma+C_M(h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-pstar))E_I, including both endpoints and the forcing contribution.

argument.text: Combine the identity and low estimate F002, the high estimate F003 and the residual bound F001. The triangle inequality and time supremum give E_I<=||e(a)||_2+C_M(h+tau)tau^gamma+C_M(N^2 h+h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-pstar))E_I for every N>=2. Discharge L1, preserving its assumptions in the antecedent, and quantify the interval and threshold to get all clauses of N010.

argument.text:
Use successive blocks of \(\lfloor\delta/\tau\rfloor\) steps, whose lengths lie in \([\delta/2,\delta]\), with a possibly shorter final block. The number of blocks is at most \(2T/\delta+1\), independently of \(\tau\). Iterating F001, starting with \(e(0)=0\), yields
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|e(t)\|_{L^2}\le C_{M,\gamma,T}\tau^\gamma, 
\]
as long as the bootstrap bound is in force. By continuity, if \(\|e\|_{L^2}\) first reached one, the same block argument up to that time would give an upper bound \(C_{M,\gamma,T}\tau^\gamma\). Choosing \(\tau_0\) smaller so that this is less than \(1/2\) gives a contradiction. Hence the accumulated block estimate holds on all of \([0,T]\). The retained initial endpoint in F003 is estimated by \(E_I\) on each block, so the recurrence also applies when \(e(a)\ne0\).
Explicitly set K=ceil(2T/delta)+1 and B_0=0, B_{j+1}=2B_j+C_M' delta. Finite induction gives B_j=C_M' delta(2^j-1). The same bound covers a truncated final block because F001 includes partial last steps. Let C0=C_M' delta(2^K-1), and choose tau0<=min(1,delta/2) with C0 tau0^gamma<1/2; gamma>0 makes this possible. At a hypothetical first hitting time ||e||_2=1, all interval suprema up to and including that time are <=1 by continuity (N001,N007), so the same finite recurrence contradicts C0 tau^gamma<1/2. Thus the bound holds on all [0,T]. At grid points N007 and Airy unitarity give ||e(t_n)||_2=||u(t_n)-u^n||_2. All constants were chosen using the common bound before selecting a datum or a grid.

# Selected target: complete Theorem 1

Source: this run's original.pdf, Theorem 1 on page 2, with the standing conventions and solution class on pages 2–3. The entire source paper, including its supplied proof, is checked-source.md.

The time grid in scheme (2) is \(\tau=T/L\), \(t_n=n\tau\), with \(L\) a positive integer and \(n=0,\ldots,L\). The maximum in Theorem 1 is over all these grid points. For fixed \(T>0\), \(0<\gamma\le1\) and \(R>0\), its \(C,\tau_0>0\) depend only on \(T,\gamma,R\) and are uniform over the specified initial-data ball and all grids with \(\tau\le\tau_0\). The theorem is for the displayed time-semidiscrete update without a spatial cutoff.

The following is the complete source statement and its standing context, transcribed from pages 2–3.

## 2 The scheme and the main result

Use normalized measure \(dx/(2\pi)\) on \(\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\); changing to unnormalized \(L^2\) only changes constants. Write \(S_t=e^{-t\partial_x^3}\), so that \(\widehat{S_tf}(k)=e^{itk^3}\widehat f(k)\). Let \(P_0\) be the mean, \(P=I-P_0\), and define \(D^{-1}=\partial_x^{-1}\) with multiplier \((ik)^{-1}\) for \(k\ne0\) and zero at zero. Set \(D^{-2}=(D^{-1})^2\). Write
\[
\widehat f(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
\|f\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\langle k\rangle^{2s}|\widehat f(k)|^2,
\qquad \langle k\rangle=(1+k^2)^{1/2}.
\]
Spaces are the completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms, with negative spaces interpreted as distributions. Orthogonality gives the normalized \(L^2\) identity for polynomials and hence for their completions. For mean-zero functions and \(s\ge0\), \(\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\le\|f\|_{H^s}\le2^{s/2}\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\); for \(s<0\), \(2^{s/2}\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\le\|f\|_{H^s}\le\|f\|_{\dot H^s}\). Real-valued means \(\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}\). All time suprema concern continuous representatives; derivative norms are essential suprema. The exact solution is the unique real mean-zero \(C([0,T];H^\gamma)\) solution obtained by smooth approximation, and satisfies the equation distributionally. The constants \(C_M\) may change from line to line and depend on \(\gamma,T,M\), but are uniform in \(n,\tau\) and spectral support.

The equation is
\[
u_t+u_{xxx}=\tfrac12\partial_x(u^2),\qquad u(0)=u_0. \tag{1}
\]
The fixed scheme is \(u^0=u_0\) and
\[
u^{n+1}=S_\tau u^n+F_\tau(u^n)+H_\tau(u^n),\qquad \tau=T/L, \tag{2}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_\tau(f)&=\tfrac16 P[(S_\tau D^{-1}f)^2]-\tfrac16 S_\tau P[(D^{-1}f)^2],\\
H_\tau(f)&=\tfrac13 P[(S_\tau D^{-1}f)D^{-1}F_\tau(f)]
+\tfrac{\tau}{9}(S_\tau D^{-1}f)P_0(f^2)\\
&\quad-\tfrac1{54}\left[S_{\tau-s}D^{-1}[(S_sD^{-1}f)^3]\right]_{s=0}^{s=\tau}\\
&\quad-\tfrac1{27\tau}\left[S_{\tau-s}D^{-2}[(S_{s-\tau}D^{-2}F_\tau(f))(S_sD^{-1}f)]\right]_{s=0}^{s=\tau}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the scheme of [1, Eq. (1.4)], without a spatial frequency cutoff.

**Theorem 1 (Logarithm-free convergence).** Let \(T>0\), \(0<\gamma\le1\), and \(R>0\). For real, mean-zero \(u_0\in H^\gamma(\mathbb T)\) with \(\|u_0\|_{H^\gamma}\le R\), there are \(C,\tau_0>0\), depending only on \(T,\gamma,R\), such that the scheme (2) satisfies
\[
\max_{0\le n\le L}\|u(n\tau)-u^n\|_{L^2}\le C\tau^\gamma
\qquad\text{whenever }\tau=T/L\le\tau_0.
\]

The periodic KdV bounds of Babin–Ilyin–Titi control the exact flow on the initial-data ball. The continuous estimates of [1, Proposition 3.4 and Lemma 7.2] will be used in the stability proof. The logarithmic convergence theorem itself is not used. For the exact twisted solution \(v(t)=S_{-t}u(t)\), set
\[
M=1+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|v(t)\|_{H^\gamma}.
\]
The source statements and the sign transformation giving a bound for \(M\) are recorded below in Section 2.1. No convergence theorem for the numerical scheme is used as an input. Intermediate constants may depend on \(M,\gamma,T\), but never on the timestep or a Fourier support bound.

<!-- PDF page 3 -->

### 2.1 The exact KdV flow

The source [2, Theorems 4.2–4.3, 5.1, 6.3–6.5] treats \(U_t=UU_x+U_{xxx}\) on the same torus, with normalized measure and mean-zero homogeneous Sobolev norms. Theorem 4.2 bounds its Galerkin flows on \([0,T]\) in \(\dot H^s\) by a constant depending only on \(s,T,\|U_0\|_{\dot H^s}\) and an upper bound for \(\|U_0\|_2\). Theorem 4.3 gives a distributional limiting solution with the same bound. Theorems 5.1 (\(s>1/2\)) and 6.3 (\(0<s\le1/2\)) give its uniqueness, \(C([0,T];\dot H^s)\) regularity and continuous dependence. Theorem 6.4 covers \(s=0\), and Theorem 6.5 with \(\theta=0\) states that, for two flows whose initial \(L^2\) norms sum to at most \(B\),
\(\sup_{[0,T]}\|U-\widetilde U\|_2\le C(T,B)\|U_0-\widetilde U_0\|_2\).
Together these results specify the continuous flow and the uniform bounds needed here.

Define \(u(t,x)=-U(t,-x)\). Then \(u_t=-U_t\), \(u_x=U_x\), \(u_{xxx}=U_{xxx}\) at \((t,-x)\), and consequently \(u_t+u_{xxx}=uu_x\). Fourier coefficients become \(\widehat u(k)=-\widehat U(-k)\), preserving every Sobolev norm, reality and zero mean. This transforms the source equation to (1). The norm comparison above transfers all bounds to our \(H^\gamma\) norm. Hence there is \(A(T,\gamma,R)<\infty\) such that every smooth initial datum in the stated ball satisfies \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u(t)\|_{H^\gamma}\le A\). The same bound holds for the limiting solution: for each finite set of frequencies pass to the limit in its finite norm sum, then take the supremum over finite sets. Thus \(M\le1+A(T,\gamma,R)\) uniformly. Continuous dependence in \(L^2\) is precisely the input used in the final density passage. No change of torus length or amplitude scaling is needed.


## Supplied proof route

The following sentences are transcribed from the supplied paper's abstract/introduction:

"The main estimate concerns the exact averaged cubic remainder. Retaining both ratios of its two oscillatory phases bounds the dual four-frequency multiplier by the reciprocal of the third largest frequency. A dyadic four-linear estimate sums this majorant without a logarithm and includes a mixed \(L^2\) endpoint. That endpoint controls the remainder at the numerical state without a numerical Sobolev bound. We then prove the full global estimate using the continuous trilinear bounds of Li and Wu, a stepwise residual calculation, low–high frequency stability, a restarted bootstrap, and density."

"In particular, the normal-form identity keeps both endpoints when the time interval is restarted, and its forcing term is estimated from the actual stepwise residual. A fixed-timestep approximation argument then removes the temporary smoothness used in the calculations."

The complete supplied proof, including all definitions, transformations, evolution equations, identities, estimates, experimental sections and bibliography, is retained in checked-source.md in original page order.
spec.conclusion: There exist C>0 and tau0>0, depending only on T,gamma,R and valid simultaneously on the whole stated initial-data ball, such that for every real mean-zero g in H^gamma(torus) with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0, the exact solution u_g (the unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) distributional KdV solution obtained by smooth approximation) and the unfiltered scheme u_g^0=g, u_g^{n+1}=Psi_tau(u_g^n) satisfy max_{0<=n<=L}||u_g(n tau)-u_g^n||_{L2}<=C tau^gamma. In particular this holds for the supplied u0, including n=0, without any spatial frequency cutoff.

For every s>=0, B0>=0, horizon b>0 and initial z0 in dot H^s with ||z0||_2<=B0, the Galerkin equations z'_k=Pi_m[(ik/2) sum_{k1+k2=k} exp(3it k k1 k2)(Pi_m z)_{k1}(Pi_m z)_{k2}], z(0)=z0, have a bound sup_{[0,b]}||z^(m)||_{dot H^s}<=K_s(b,B0,||z0||_{dot H^s}), uniformly in m (Theorem 4.2); the proof supplies a bound uniform when the indicated initial norm is bounded. For s>0 and 0<sigma<s, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,b];dot H^sigma), 1<p<infinity, and weak-star in L-infinity dot H^s to a weak solution with the same bound and L2 conservation a.e. (4.3). This solution is unique and C([0,b];dot H^s), with Lipschitz continuous dependence in dot H^s, and conserves L2 at every time: for s>1/2 by 5.1, for 0<s<=1/2 by 6.3. For s=0 there is likewise a unique C([0,b];L2) weak solution with Lipschitz dependence (6.4). For any theta in (-1,0], and any two flows with ||z0||_2+||w0||_2<=B0, sup_{[0,b]}||z-w||_{dot H^theta}<=C' C_{B0}^b ||z0-w0||_{dot H^theta}, where C',C_{B0} depend only on B0,theta (6.5). The real, zero-mean class and normalized measure are standing conditions throughout.

propositions.statement: There is a finite A(T,gamma,R) uniform for every real mean-zero datum g with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R. Its KdV equation u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2), u(0)=g, has a unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) solution obtained by smooth approximation, solving the equation distributionally, with sup_t||u(t)||_{H^gamma}<=A. Smooth data give spatially smooth solutions. For v(t)=S_{-t}u(t), v'=B_t(v,v)/2 and all Sobolev norms of v and u agree. For two such exact flows with initial L2 norms summing to at most B0, sup_t||u-tilde u||_2<=C(T,B0)||g-tilde g||_2. In particular M=1+sup_t||v(t)||_{H^gamma}<=1+A uniformly.

argument.text: H001 supplies the positive horizon and 0<gamma<=1. Apply E001 with s=gamma, horizon T, initial L2 bound R and initial dot H^gamma bound R, to arbitrary real mean-zero data in that ball. The source has normalized measure. It gives a bound uniform over these bounded norms and a solution. Its uniqueness/continuity branch is 5.1 for gamma>1/2 and 6.3 for 0<gamma<=1/2. The source theta=0 estimate gives uniform L2 dependence with initial sum bound B0. These applications concern only exact flows, not scheme convergence.

produces.statement: For the source sign of KdV, the real mean-zero H^gamma ball has a uniform finite homogeneous Sobolev bound and a unique continuous flow; pairs have the E001 theta=0 L2 dependence bound. Smooth data give smooth flows by applying the same existence and uniqueness results at every integer Sobolev exponent.

argument.text: Define \(u(t,x)=-U(t,-x)\). Then \(u_t=-U_t\), \(u_x=U_x\), \(u_{xxx}=U_{xxx}\) at \((t,-x)\), and consequently \(u_t+u_{xxx}=uu_x\). Fourier coefficients become \(\widehat u(k)=-\widehat U(-k)\), preserving every Sobolev norm, reality and zero mean. This transforms the source equation to (1). The norm comparison above transfers all bounds to our \(H^\gamma\) norm. Hence there is \(A(T,\gamma,R)<\infty\) such that every smooth initial datum in the stated ball satisfies \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u(t)\|_{H^\gamma}\le A\). The same bound holds for the limiting solution: for each finite set of frequencies pass to the limit in its finite norm sum, then take the supremum over finite sets. Thus \(M\le1+A(T,\gamma,R)\) uniformly. Continuous dependence in \(L^2\) is precisely the input used in the final density passage. No change of torus length or amplitude scaling is needed. More explicitly, the physical change u(t,x)=-U(t,-x) maps initial data g to source initial data -g(-x), so preserves the whole initial-data ball. The homogeneous-to-inhomogeneous inequalities follow coefficientwise from |k|<=<k><=sqrt(2)|k| for k!=0. For a continuous limiting flow the finite-frequency sums and then their supremum give the bound at each time, with the same constant. Apply the source pair bound after this isometry; it gives the stated C(T,B0) bound. Twisting by S_{-t} differentiates away -partial_x^3 and gives v'=B_t(v,v)/2. This proves all clauses of N001, for arbitrary data in the ball.

applications.bindings: Set source s=gamma, b=T, B0=R and source initial datum -g(-x). For continuity use 5.1 if gamma>1/2 and 6.3 otherwise; for smooth persistence use each positive integer s. For pairs set theta=0 and B0 to their initial norm sum bound.
hypothesis_checks: H001 gives T>0 and gamma>0; real mean-zero data g in the ball remain real mean-zero with the same norms after sign/reflection. Their L2 and dot H^gamma norms are <=R by coefficientwise norm comparison. For smooth data every integer Sobolev norm is finite, so uniqueness identifies those regular flows.
theta=0 belongs to (-1,0]. The two initial L2 norms are, by the universally stated pair condition, bounded in sum by B0. Reflection preserves this sum.

argument.text:
Fix tau>0 and real phases alpha,beta. Also, independently, fix a nonzero integer quadruple of zero sum. Assume L1 to collect these antecedent conditions. If either phase vanishes its covariance vanishes by its definition. For the remaining phase case use the following calculation.
 Let \(h(s)=e^{-i\alpha s}-M_\tau(e^{-i\alpha s})\). Then \(\eta_\tau=\tau^{-1}\int_0^\tau h(s)e^{-i\beta s}\,ds\). The elementary bound
\(|h(s)|\le\tau^{-1}\int_0^\tau|\alpha||s-r|\,dr\le\tau|\alpha|\)
gives the linear phase bound in N002, also interchanging \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Moreover,
\[
|h(0)|+|h(\tau)|\le\tau|\alpha|,\qquad
\int_0^\tau|h'(s)|\,ds=\tau|\alpha|.
\]
Integrating \(e^{-i\beta s}\) once gives \(|\eta_\tau|\le2|\alpha/\beta|\). Interchanging the phases proves the ratio bound in N002.

produces.statement: For these phases, eta=0 if alpha beta=0, and otherwise |eta|<=2 min(|alpha/beta|,|beta/alpha|) and |eta|<=tau min(|alpha|,|beta|).

argument.text:
For the quadruple let A=|ab|, B0=|cd| and N1>=N2>=N3>=N4 be the sorted magnitudes. The largest magnitude is at most the sum of the other three, hence N1<=3N2.
 For the required ratio majorant, if \(d\) is among the two largest frequencies, use \(\min(A/B0,B0/A)\le1\). Otherwise the largest two are among \(a,b,c\). If they are \(a,b\), then
\[
\frac1{|d|}\min(A/B0,B0/A)\le\frac{|c|}{|ab|}\le\frac1{N_3}.
\]
If they are \(a,c\) (the case \(b,c\) is identical), their ratio is between \(1/3\) and \(3\). The remaining magnitudes are \(|b|,|d|\), whose maximum is \(N_3\). Thus
\[
\frac1{|d|}\min(A/B0,B0/A)\le3\min\left\{\frac{|b|}{|d|^2},\frac1{|b|}\right\}
\le\frac3{\max(|b|,|d|)}.
\]
For the required sum majorant, consider the pairing \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\). If the two largest magnitudes are in the same pair, the other pair has sum of magnitude at most \(2N_3\). Since \(a+b=-(c+d)\),
\[
\frac{|a+b|}{\max(A,B0)}\le\frac{2N_3}{N_1N_2}\le\frac2{N_3}.
\]
If the largest two belong to different pairs, the third largest is paired with one of them. Hence \(\max(A,B0)\ge N_2N_3\) and \(|a+b|\le2N_1\le6N_2\), giving the result. Ties can be ordered arbitrarily; the same alternatives cover them. 
This covers all placements and ties. Discharge L1 and universally quantify both independent choices to obtain N002.

argument.text:
Fix four nonnegative ell2 sequences, under temporary antecedent L1.  It suffices first to consider finitely supported sequences. Decompose into shells \(2^j\le|k|<2^{j+1}\), \(j\ge0\), and write \(Xshell_{r,j}\) for the \(\ell^2\) norm of the \(r\)th sequence on the \(j\)th shell. Fix an ordering of the four shell indices \(j_1\ge j_2\ge j_3\ge j_4\). A nonzero zero-sum interaction has \(j_1-j_2\le2\). For each fixed pair of smaller-shell frequencies, the remaining sum of the two larger-shell sequences is at most their \(\ell^2\) norm product by Cauchy–Schwarz, since one sequence is a translated reflection of the other. Sum the smaller frequencies in \(\ell^1\). A shell has at most \(2^{j+1}\) integer elements, so another Cauchy–Schwarz bound gives
\[
\sum_{a+b+c+d=0}\prod_{r=1}^4 x_{r,j_r}
\le C2^{(j_3+j_4)/2}\prod_{r=1}^4 Xshell_{r,j_r}.
\]
Since \(N_3\ge2^{j_3}\), the weight leaves \(C2^{-(j_3-j_4)/2}\). For \(q=j_1-j_2\in\{0,1,2\}\), extend the nonnegative sum by dropping the upper restriction on the smaller shells. The contribution is at most
\[
C\left(\sum_{J0} Xshell_{1,J0}Xshell_{2,J0-q}\right)
\left(\sum_{\ell\ge m}2^{-(\ell-m)/2}Xshell_{3,\ell}Xshell_{4,m}\right).
\]
The first factor is bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz. Writing \(r=\ell-m\), the second is at most
\[
\sum_{r\ge0}2^{-r/2}\|Xshell_3\|_{\ell^2}\|Xshell_4\|_{\ell^2}
=\frac{\|Xshell_3\|_{\ell^2}\|Xshell_4\|_{\ell^2}}{1-2^{-1/2}}.
\]
Sum over at most 24 orderings and three offsets. For arbitrary nonnegative sequences apply the finite bound to their restrictions to \(|k|\le m\). The infinite positive sum is the supremum of these finite sums, while the norms of the restrictions are bounded by the full norms. This proves the infinite statement without exchanging conditionally convergent sums. 
Restriction to a subset only decreases the nonnegative sum. Discharge L1 to obtain the universally quantified N003.

argument.text:
H001 supplies 0<gamma<=1 for the final numerical-state specialization. Independently fix lambda in [0,1], tau>0, step time t_n, and mean-zero polynomial inputs. Temporarily assume these range conditions as L1. Use the following computation with the proof's letter gamma replaced everywhere by lambda; no numerical state regularity is assumed.
 Only nonzero \(abck\) and \(p=a+b\ne0\) need consideration. Set \(d=-k\). N002 and the first majorant in N002 give
\[
\frac{|\eta|}{|k|}\le\frac6{N_3}.
\]
For the other endpoint, observe that \(AB=|abck|\), and use the linear phase bound in N002 and the second majorant in N002:
\[
\frac{|\eta|}{\tau|abck|}\le3\frac{|p|\min(A,B)}{AB}
=3\frac{|p|}{\max(A,B)}\le\frac{18}{N_3}.
\]
Taking the geometric mean of these two bounds yields
\[
\boxed{\frac{|\eta_\tau(\alpha,\beta)|}{|k||abc|^\lambda}
\le\frac{6^{1-\lambda}18^\lambda\tau^\lambda}{N_3(a,b,c,-k)}.} 
\]



Dualize the remainder definition D014 against an \(\ell^2\) sequence and take absolute values. Apply N003 with \(x_1(a)=|a|^\lambda|\widehat f_1(a)|\) and analogously for \(x_2,x_3\); \(x_4(d)\) is the absolute value of the dual coefficient at \(-d\). Their norms are bounded by the inhomogeneous Sobolev norms and the dual norm. The factors \(e^{-it_n\Phi}\) have modulus one. This proves the theorem, including the assertion about restricted sums. Polynomial approximation and the bound extend the operator to the claimed spaces. 
Here the two estimates used are directly N002 and the four-linear estimate is N003. At lambda=0 or 1 use the corresponding endpoint directly, so no 0^0 convention is needed.

produces.statement: For each lambda in [0,1], polynomial mean-zero inputs obey the stated restricted-multiplier bound with constant independent of support; the displayed endpoint interpolation gives |eta|/(|k||abc|^lambda)<=6^(1-lambda)18^lambda tau^lambda/N3.

argument.text:
The polynomial estimate F001 makes each Cauchy approximation converge in L2: expand a trilinear difference into three terms and apply the same bound. It gives a unique continuous trilinear extension to the mean-zero H^lambda completions and preserves the multiplier restrictions. For the numerical-state estimate fix mean-zero w in H^gamma, f in L2, ||w||_{H^gamma}<=M, delta=||f-w||_2<=1, and 0<tau<=1.  Apply F001 at lambda=gamma with exponent \(\gamma\) to \((w,w,w)\). Expand the difference between the cubic expressions at \(f\) and at \(w\), and apply F001 at lambda=0 to every difference term. This gives \(C\tau\delta(\|f\|_{L^2}+\|w\|_{L^2})^2\). No \(H^\gamma\) bound on the numerical state is used. 
Indeed ||f||_2<=M+1, so the difference is bounded by C_M tau delta, while the value at w is <=C M^3 tau^(1+gamma). These establish both assertions. Discharge L1 and the stated conditional specialization, retaining all its conditions in the output.

argument.text: Use H001. For E002 take arbitrary I=[a,b] subset [0,T] with b-a<=1 and lambda=0 for the X estimate. X gives precisely L-infinity L2 and L-infinity H^(-23/14) derivative, its hypotheses. Its three choices of negative-norm slot are retained. For constant inputs use E002 with any lambda in [0,1]. Each source spatial norm is sqrt(2 pi) times ours: divide by sqrt(2 pi) on the output and absorb the remaining product factors 2 pi into the constant. This proves the first two assertions without changing their exponent or time length. Smooth or continuous piecewise smooth time functions have the stated distributional derivative, so E002 applies directly. General X inputs use the source bounded interpretation of the operator.

argument.text:
For the product and stages use E003 with lambda=gamma and epsilon=1/8 at gamma=1/2. The diagonal bilinear stage is exactly F_n(t;w), by definition. The necessary source exponent checks and retained calculations are:
when \(\|w\|_{H^\gamma}\le M\). One can take \(a_\gamma=1/2-\gamma\) for \(0<\gamma<1/2\), \(1/8\) for \(\gamma=1/2\), and \(a_\gamma=0\) for \(\gamma>1/2\). For clarity, the source stage exponent is \(\theta=(1+\gamma-\beta)/(1+\gamma-\beta_0)\), with \(\beta_0=2\gamma-3/2\) for \(0<\gamma<1/2\), \(\beta_0=-1/2-\epsilon\) for \(\gamma=1/2\), and \(\beta_0=\gamma-1\) for \(1/2<\gamma\le1\). Take \(\epsilon=1/8\) in the middle case. At \(\beta=a_\gamma\) the exponents are respectively \((1/2+2\gamma)/(5/2-\gamma)\ge\gamma\), \(11/17>1/2\) and \((1+\gamma)/2\ge\gamma\). Every \(a_\gamma\) lies in the source interval \([\beta_0,1+\gamma]\). Since \(0<\tau\le1\), these exponents imply the first bound in the asserted stage inequalities. At \(\beta=1+\gamma\) the exponent is zero, giving the second. Inequality the asserted product inequality is the source E003, with the same fixed \(1/8\) choice when \(\gamma=1/2\). Source \(L^2\) and \(H^s\) norms are \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) times ours; dividing the source inequalities absorbs only fixed factors into constants. These estimates require no regularity beyond \(H^\gamma\) on \(w\). Finally the elementary one-dimensional bounds are
For the first range the exponent inequality reduces to gamma^2-gamma/2+1/2=(gamma-1/4)^2+7/16>0; at gamma=1/2 the exponent is 11/17 and in the last range (1+gamma)/2>=gamma. Thus both stage conclusions follow uniformly for 0<tau<=1. All relevant bounds and the product inequality have now been proved in the declared normalization.
